Fix integers $t\ge2$ and $b\ge1$. There are $b$ blocks, each containing the
same $t$ fixed experimental units, indexed within block $j$ by
$i\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. The $t$ treatments form a fixed set $\mathcal T$ with
$|\mathcal T|=t$. A **complete block** is a block in which each treatment is
assigned to exactly one unit. The blocks and their units are fixed before
randomization.

Let $S_t$ be the set of permutations from the unit labels to $\mathcal T$.
The **randomized complete-block design (RCBD)** uses assignment space
$\mathcal Z=(S_t)^b$ and the uniform probability law on this finite nonempty
set. Thus each $z=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_b)$ has probability $(t!)^{-b}$; the
within-block treatment permutations are independent and individually uniform.
This is a finite randomized-treatment assignment model
([[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]]) whose units are the
$tb$ cells and whose assignment is the only randomness supplied by the
design. The design specifies no response model, Gaussian errors, additivity,
or absence of interference. A pair is the special case $t=2,b=1$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $V$ be a vector
space over $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $U$ be a family of linear subspaces
$U_i$ of $V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) with

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$$

([[def-internal-direct-sum]]) and every $U_i$ finite-dimensional over $F$
([[def-dimension]]). Then $V$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and

$$\dim_F V \;=\; \sum_{i<n} \dim_F U_i ,$$

the right-hand side being the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read
additively in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{N}, +, 0)$
([[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-add-identity]],
[[lem-nat-add-associative]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]]).

**The base case is a genuine case.** At $n = 0$ the direct sum of the empty
family is $\{0_V\}$ and the empty sum of natural numbers is $0$, so the formula
reads $\dim_F\{0_V\} = 0$. **At $n = 2$** it reads
$\dim_F(U \oplus W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$.

**No choice principle is used.** The only inputs are
[[thm-dimension-formula]] and [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], both of
which are proved in finite dimension without one.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$. Its **row space** $\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq F^n$ is the span of its rows, its **column space** $\operatorname{Col}(A)\subseteq F^m$ is the span of its columns, and its **nullspace** is
$$N(A):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=0\}.$$

The **row rank** and **column rank** are
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Row}(A),\qquad \operatorname{crank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Col}(A).$$
These dimensions are defined because each space is spanned by a finite list.
Starting with the empty list, inspect the spanning vectors in order and retain a
vector exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. Induction
shows that the retained list is independent and has the same span as the
original finite list, so it is a finite basis. The **rank** of $A$ is its row
rank; [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] proves that it also equals the column
rank.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

derivations.claim: Let $H=\{a\in\mathbb R^t:\mathbf1_t^Ta=0\}$. The coordinate-sum map $\mathbb R^t\to\mathbb R$ is onto, so [F2] gives $\dim H=t-1$. By [F6], $\dim\operatorname{row}(C)=\dim\operatorname{im}C=\operatorname{rank}C=q$. For every $a\in\mathbb R^t$, the vector $h=a-(\mathbf1_t^Ta/t)\mathbf1_t$ lies in $H$ and satisfies $Ch=Ca$, because $C\mathbf1_t=0$. Thus $\operatorname{im}(C|_H)=\operatorname{im}C$ has dimension $q$, and [F2] gives $\dim(H\cap\ker C)=t-1-q$. The row space of $C$ lies in $H$ and is orthogonal to $H\cap\ker C$. The orthogonal complement of $H\cap\ker C$ within $H$ has dimension $q$: both subspaces are finite-dimensional by [F4], and [F3]–[F5] subtract dimensions from $\dim H=t-1$. Since this complement contains the $q$-dimensional row space, the equality case of [F4] identifies it with that row space.

In $V$, the constant arrays form a one-dimensional space $G$, the arrays $(a_i)_{ij}$ for $a\in H$ form a $(t-1)$-dimensional treatment space $T$, and the arrays $(d_j)_{ij}$ for $d\in\mathbb R^b$ with $\sum_jd_j=0$ form a $(b-1)$-dimensional block space $B$. The replication maps from the two zero-sum coordinate spaces to $T$ and $B$ are linear bijections: their repeated rows or columns recover the original coordinates, so they transport bases and give the stated dimensions; the block zero-sum space has dimension $b-1$ by [F2] applied to its onto coordinate-sum map. These spaces are pairwise orthogonal: the treatment-block inner product is $\sum_{i,j}a_id_j=(\sum_i a_i)(\sum_jd_j)=0$, and either zero-sum condition also makes the relevant inner product with $G$ zero. Their sum is direct: if three mutually orthogonal vectors sum to zero, taking the inner product with each one gives its squared norm zero. Thus $W_U=G\oplus T\oplus B$, and the finite-dimensional direct-sum formula [F5] gives $\dim W_U=1+(t-1)+(b-1)=t+b-1$. The reduced space replaces $T$ by the replicated arrays from $H\cap\ker C$, whose dimension is $t-1-q$ by step 1.1; the same formula gives $\dim W_R(C)=1+(t-1-q)+(b-1)=t+b-1-q$.

For any $y$, set $r_{ij}=y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot j}+\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$. Summing $r$ over any row gives zero because $\sum_j y_{ij}=b\bar y_{i\cdot}$ and $\sum_j\bar y_{\cdot j}=b\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$; summing over any column likewise gives zero. Conversely, if $v$ is orthogonal to $T$, then its row-sum vector is orthogonal to every $a\in H$, so all row sums are equal; orthogonality to $G$ makes their total zero, so every row sum is zero. The same argument with $B$ gives zero column sums. Thus $W_U^\perp=E$. Also $(y-r)_{ij}=\bar y_{i\cdot}+\bar y_{\cdot j}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$ belongs to $W_U$. By [F3], this is the orthogonal decomposition of $y$ relative to $W_U$, proving the formula for $RSS_U$; the subspace $E$ is finite-dimensional by [F4], and [F3] gives $V=W_U\oplus E$. Since the standard cell-coordinate basis makes $\dim V=tb$, [F5] gives $\dim E=tb-(t+b-1)=(t-1)(b-1)$.

Put $P_C=C^T(CC^T)^{-1}C$. The matrix $CC^T$ is invertible since $C$ has full row rank. Direct multiplication gives $P_C^T=P_C$, $P_C^2=P_C$, and image $P_C=\operatorname{row}(C)$. For any $x$ and $a\in\mathbb R^q$, $\langle x-P_Cx,C^Ta\rangle=a^TCx-a^TCC^T(CC^T)^{-1}Cx=0$, so [F3] identifies $P_C$ as the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{row}(C)$. Consequently $T$ is the orthogonal direct sum of the reduced treatment space and the treatment arrays formed from $\operatorname{row}(C)$. Therefore $W_U=W_R(C)\oplus D_C$, where $D_C=\{(a_i)_{ij}:a\in\operatorname{row}(C)\}$.

The projection of $y$ onto $D_C$ is the array repeating $P_C\bar y$ across all $b$ blocks: its residual is orthogonal to every repeated $a\in\operatorname{row}(C)$ because the inner product is $b\,a^T(\bar y-P_C\bar y)=0$. Its squared norm is $b\|P_C\bar y\|^2=b(C\bar y)^T(CC^T)^{-1}(C\bar y)$. In the orthogonal direct sum of step 3.2, $y-P_{W_R}y$ is this projection plus $y-P_{W_U}y$, and the two parts are orthogonal; expanding the squared norm gives the claimed residual-sum reduction.

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent. Their values are
**substantively untestable** from the observed-data law; the
assignment-invariance claim is a hypothesis tested by the theorem, not an
empirical fact supplied by the design. These classifications do not make
the design or scientific model empirically true.

[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]] in which the allowed
assignment set is $\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ and unit $i$'s response under

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Embed the pair's design law in the finite binary assignment model on $\{0,1\}^2$ by giving weight $1/2$ to $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ and weight zero to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. Zero-probability assignments are allowed by [F1]. The positive-weight assignments give the displayed $D_1,D_2$, with average $(\delta_1+\delta_2)/2$ and difference $(\delta_1-\delta_2)+2(Y_1(0)-Y_2(0))$.

Define $D$ by the treated-minus-control formula on the two positive-weight assignments and, for example, by zero on the two zero-weight assignments. This is a function on the full-power-set data space [F7], hence a measurable statistic and estimator of $\tau$ by [F6]; its arbitrary zero-weight values do not affect design moments.
By [F4], $\mathbb E_d[D]=(D_1+D_2)/2=(\delta_1+\delta_2)/2=\tau$, so the contrast estimates the pair's finite-population average effect without bias.

Let $X$ indicate that unit $1$ is assigned treatment $1$, so $D=D_2+(D_1-D_2)X$. Since the assignment space is finite, the variables are square-integrable. By [F5] and [F8], covariance with a constant is zero and $\operatorname{Var}_d(D)=(D_1-D_2)^2\operatorname{Var}_d(X)$.

The two equally weighted assignments give $\mathbb E_d[X]=1/2$ by [F4], hence $\operatorname{Var}_d(X)=1/4$ by [F5]. Therefore $\operatorname{Var}_d(D)=(D_1-D_2)^2/4$, which is the formula in the Statement.

rank $q$ and satisfy $C\mathbf 1_t=0$. Give $V=\mathbb R^{t\times b}$ the
Frobenius inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i,j}u_{ij}v_{ij}$. Write
$\operatorname{row}(C)=\operatorname{im}(C^T)$ for the span of the rows of $C$,
and define the full additive mean space
$$W_U=\{(\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j)_{ij}:\mu\in\mathbb R,\ \sum_i\tau_i=0,\ \sum_j\beta_j=0\}$$
and the reduced space $W_R(C)$ by the same formula with the extra restriction
$C\tau=0$. For an array $y$, write
$\bar y_{i\cdot}=b^{-1}\sum_jy_{ij}$,
$\bar y_{\cdot j}=t^{-1}\sum_iy_{ij}$, and
$\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}=(tb)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}y_{ij}$. Let
$RSS_U=\|y-P_{W_U}y\|^2$ and $RSS_R=\|y-P_{W_R(C)}y\|^2$, where $P_W$ is
the orthogonal projection onto $W$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). Then
$$\dim W_U=t+b-1,\qquad \dim W_R(C)=t+b-1-q,$$
$$W_U^\perp=E:=\{r\in\mathbb R^{t\times b}:\sum_jr_{ij}=0\text{ for every }i,\ \sum_ir_{ij}=0\text{ for every }j\},\qquad \dim E=(t-1)(b-1),$$
$$RSS_U=\sum_{i,j}(y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot j}+\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2,$$
and
$$RSS_R-RSS_U=b(C\bar y)^T(CC^T)^{-1}(C\bar y),$$
where $\bar y=(\bar y_{1\cdot},\ldots,\bar y_{t\cdot})^T$.

Fix integers $t\ge2$ and $b\ge1$. There are $b$ blocks, each containing the
same $t$ fixed experimental units, indexed within block $j$ by
$i\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. The $t$ treatments form a fixed set $\mathcal T$ with
$|\mathcal T|=t$. A **complete block** is a block in which each treatment is
assigned to exactly one unit. The blocks and their units are fixed before
randomization.

Let $S_t$ be the set of permutations from the unit labels to $\mathcal T$.
The **randomized complete-block design (RCBD)** uses assignment space
$\mathcal Z=(S_t)^b$ and the uniform probability law on this finite nonempty
set. Thus each $z=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_b)$ has probability $(t!)^{-b}$; the
within-block treatment permutations are independent and individually uniform.
This is a finite randomized-treatment assignment model
([[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]]) whose units are the
$tb$ cells and whose assignment is the only randomness supplied by the
design. The design specifies no response model, Gaussian errors, additivity,
or absence of interference. A pair is the special case $t=2,b=1$.

derivations.claim: Write the cell array as $Y=m+\gamma+\epsilon$, where $m\in W_U$ is additive and $\gamma\in E$. By [F1], the residual from projection onto $W_U$ is $(I-P_{W_U})Y=\gamma+(I-P_{W_U})\epsilon$, and the latter error projection lies in $E=W_U^\perp$.

The additive space has dimension $t+b-1$ and $E$ has dimension $(t-1)(b-1)$, so their orthogonal direct sum has dimension $tb$, the full cell-space dimension. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n>p\ge1$ whose $p$ columns are linearly independent. Use the experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$, with observation $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Define the least-squares statistic and residual sum of squares by
$$\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p},\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
For every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$\widetilde T_c:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,$$
and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$, with $S>0$ almost surely.

For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. Under the null hypothesis that the mean vector belongs to $W_R$,
$$\widetilde F:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)},&RSS_U>0,\\ 0,&RSS_U=0 \end{cases} \sim F_{q,n-p}.$$
The numerator and denominator chi-square contributions are independent. All t and F denominator degrees of freedom in the statement are positive.

Let $t,b\ge2$, $1\le q\le t-1$, and let $C\in\mathbb R^{q\times t}$ have
rank $q$ and satisfy $C\mathbf 1_t=0$. Give $V=\mathbb R^{t\times b}$ the
Frobenius inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i,j}u_{ij}v_{ij}$. Write
$\operatorname{row}(C)=\operatorname{im}(C^T)$ for the span of the rows of $C$,
and define the full additive mean space
$$W_U=\{(\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j)_{ij}:\mu\in\mathbb R,\ \sum_i\tau_i=0,\ \sum_j\beta_j=0\}$$
and the reduced space $W_R(C)$ by the same formula with the extra restriction
$C\tau=0$. For an array $y$, write
$\bar y_{i\cdot}=b^{-1}\sum_jy_{ij}$,
$\bar y_{\cdot j}=t^{-1}\sum_iy_{ij}$, and
$\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}=(tb)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}y_{ij}$. Let
$RSS_U=\|y-P_{W_U}y\|^2$ and $RSS_R=\|y-P_{W_R(C)}y\|^2$, where $P_W$ is
the orthogonal projection onto $W$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). Then
$$\dim W_U=t+b-1,\qquad \dim W_R(C)=t+b-1-q,$$
$$W_U^\perp=E:=\{r\in\mathbb R^{t\times b}:\sum_jr_{ij}=0\text{ for every }i,\ \sum_ir_{ij}=0\text{ for every }j\},\qquad \dim E=(t-1)(b-1),$$
$$RSS_U=\sum_{i,j}(y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot j}+\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2,$$
and
$$RSS_R-RSS_U=b(C\bar y)^T(CC^T)^{-1}(C\bar y),$$
where $\bar y=(\bar y_{1\cdot},\ldots,\bar y_{t\cdot})^T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$ and are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the complementary Borel nonpositive-denominator region is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent. Their values are
**substantively untestable** from the observed-data law; the
assignment-invariance claim is a hypothesis tested by the theorem, not an
empirical fact supplied by the design. These classifications do not make
the design or scientific model empirically true.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $W_R(C)\subset W_U$, $p=\dim W_U=t+b-1$, $q=\dim W_U-\dim W_R(C)$, and $n=tb$. Since $t,b\ge2$, $n-p=tb-t-b+1=(t-1)(b-1)=\nu>0$, and $q\le t-1\le p$. Under $C\tau=0$, the mean array $(\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j)_{ij}$ belongs to $W_R(C)$. Thus the nested-space, positive-degree, and null-mean hypotheses of [F1] hold.

Applying [F1] gives the piecewise nested-model statistic $\{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q\}/\{RSS_U/\nu\}$ the law $F_{q,\nu}$, with its value set to zero when $RSS_U=0$. The finite assignment law [F5] supplies no normal-error assumption; Gaussianity here is separately imposed in the Given. AC is used exactly through [A1] and [F1].

By [F2], the numerator reduction is $b(C\bar Y)^T(CC^T)^{-1}(C\bar Y)$, so the statistic in the Statement is the same piecewise ratio. Its numerator and residual sum of squares are continuous functions of the data, and the ratio with the stated zero-denominator branch is Borel measurable; hence it is a statistic by [F4].
Since $q,\nu>0$, [F3] defines the named central law and step 3.1 is the piecewise nested-model ratio from [F1]. It therefore has law $F_{q,\nu}$, as claimed.

Fix $t\ge1$ and put $R_t=\{0,1,\ldots,t-1\}$, with addition interpreted
modulo $t$. A **Latin-square allocation of order $t$** is a function
$L:R_t\times R_t\to R_t$ such that for
each fixed row the map from columns to treatments is a bijection, and for
each fixed column the map from rows to treatments is a bijection. Thus each
treatment occurs exactly once in every row and every column. Let
$\mathcal L_t$ be the finite set of these allocations and assign the uniform
law on $\mathcal L_t$. This law is well-defined: $L_0(r,c)=r+c\pmod t$ is a
Latin square, since adding a fixed residue modulo $t$ permutes the residues; hence
$\mathcal L_t$ is nonempty. This specifies one exact
restricted randomization law. It randomizes over treatment-by-row-by-column
assignments and, for $t\ge2$, is distinct from the product of independent
within-block permutations in an RCBD ([[def-randomized-complete-block-design]]).

In the repeated-row array, each row contains $A,B,C$ once, so it is an RCBD assignment; each column repeats a single treatment, so it is not a Latin square.

There are $3!=6$ permutations per RCBD block and the blocks are independently uniform, so the particular repeated-row assignment has probability $6^{-3}=1/216$. It has probability zero under a law supported only on Latin squares.

the double-centered arrays
$$E=\{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{t\times b}:\sum_j\gamma_{ij}=0\ \text{for every }i,\ \sum_i\gamma_{ij}=0\ \text{for every }j\},$$
which has dimension $(t-1)(b-1)$ ([[lem-rcbd-nested-contrast-model-and-projection]]).
If a treatment-by-block interaction $\gamma\in E$ is included in the mean,

interaction and projected error, and fitting the unrestricted interaction
leaves zero pure-error residual degrees of freedom. This is an algebraic
design limitation; it does not assert nonidentifiability under every
additional stochastic model.

Consider one pair in the $t=2,b=1$ RCBD, with the two treatments labelled
$0$ and $1$. Let $Y_\ell(z)\in\mathbb R$ be unit $\ell$'s fixed potential
outcome under its own treatment $z\in\{0,1\}$, and assume no interference:
the outcome depends on the pair assignment only through that unit's own
treatment. Define $\delta_\ell=Y_\ell(1)-Y_\ell(0)$,
$\tau=(\delta_1+\delta_2)/2$, and the two possible observed contrasts
$$D_1=Y_1(1)-Y_2(0),\qquad D_2=Y_2(1)-Y_1(0).$$
If exactly one unit is assigned treatment $1$ uniformly at random, the
observed treated-minus-control contrast $D$ obeys
$$\mathbb E_d[D]=\tau,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_d(D)=\frac{(D_1-D_2)^2}{4}=\frac{\bigl((\delta_1-\delta_2)+2(Y_1(0)-Y_2(0))\bigr)^2}{4}.$$
Here $\mathbb E_d$ and $\operatorname{Var}_d$ average over treatment
assignment only, holding all potential outcomes fixed. The variance depends
on baseline outcomes as well as effect heterogeneity.

In the two-unit, two-treatment paired randomization, let
$\delta_\ell=Y_\ell(1)-Y_\ell(0)$ and
$\tau=(\delta_1+\delta_2)/2$. Define $S$ to be the fixed treatment effect
$\delta_\ell$ of whichever unit $\ell$ is assigned treatment $1$. Then
$$\mathbb E_d[S]=\tau,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_d(S)=\frac{(\delta_1-\delta_2)^2}{4}.$$
The random variable $S$ uses both potential outcomes of the selected unit;
it is not the observed treated-minus-control contrast and is not a statistic
of the observed assignment and response data.
